catalog_quote: Although tonal contrast is found in virtually all of the the Lakes Plain languages, it will not be shown in the word list transcriptions. Additionally, stress is not marked because only a few original word lists marked it and it has not been found to be contrastive in any of the Lakes Plain languages to date. [p.152, sec. 11 Tone typology:] Tone is a prominent feature of all Lakes Plain languages and therefore was most likely a feature of some of the protolanguages as well. ... All the modern languages have at least high and low tone. Duvle and Sikaritai have only these tones with Martin (1991) analysing the Sikaritai system as pitch-accent. The remainder of the languages also have combinations of high and low (or contours); Obokuitai has a fall (Jenison 1991), Doutai (McAllister 1991), Edopi (Kim 1995) and all the western Tariku languages have a fall and a rise (Clouse n.d.1).

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Copies checked: and its extracted text;; I appended a dated independent-check note). QUOTE: lines 1327-1331 (p.160, Appendix 3 intro, running head '160 DUANE A. CLOUSE') read exactly: 'Although tonal contrast is found in virtually all of the the Lakes Plain languages, it will not be shown in the word list transcriptions. Additionally, stress is not marked because only a few original word lists marked it and it has not been found to be contrastive in any of the Lakes Plain languages to date.' -- verbatim including the doubled 'the the'. The p.152 sec. 11 'Tone typology' portion (lines 928-935) is also there: 'Tone is a prominent feature of all Lakes Plain languages.. All the modem languages…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Fayu, like all Lakes Plain languages, is a lexical tone language (West Tariku: H, L plus falling and rising contours; Kuegler 1989 via Yoder 2020 gives L, H, HL, ML for Fayu specifically). Stress has not been found contrastive in any Lakes Plain language; no rule for the position of (non-contrastive) stress in Fayu is stated anywhere I could open.
new_statements.exceptions: None; the statement is a family-wide generalisation ('to date'), not a Fayu-specific analysis.
new_statements.domain_note: Statement concerns word-list transcription across the family; no word- vs phrase-level discussion. Fayu-specific suprasegmental analysis exists only in Kuegler's unpublished SIL ms and (presumably) Maitland 2020, neither accessible.
new_statements.identity_note: Clouse 1997 treats Fayu as one language with two dialects, (a) Fayu and (b) Sehudate (81% cognate); his Fayu wordlist is Kuegler's, village Foida, c. 1986. The quoted stress statement is family-wide (all Lakes Plain), not specific to either dialect. Glottolog fayu1238 lists Sehudate as an alternative name.
